svg.text: SDP: depend in the direction of stability
stability is the work needed to change something (a penny on its side is unstable
though it does not change; a table is stable); the surest way to make a component
hard to change is to have many depend on it. X: three dependents (responsible), no
dependencies (independent): stable. Y: no dependents (irresponsible), three
dependencies (dependent): unstable. Fan-in counts classes outside that depend on
classes inside; Fan-out the reverse; I = Fan-out / (Fan-in + Fan-out), 0 maximally
stable, 1 maximally unstable
Applying SDP
I should decrease in the direction of dependency (Cc: fan-in 3, fan-out 1, I = 1/4;
in C++ count #include, in Java imports); not all components should be stable: put
changeable ones on top, stable below (arrows pointing up violate SDP and ADP); fix
a violation (Stable depends on Flexible's class C used by U) with DIP: an interface
US in a new UServer component (I = 0) that C implements; such abstract components
are common in static languages and absent in dynamic ones
SAP: a component should be as abstract as it is stable
put high-level policy in stable components (I = 0) and keep them extensible through
abstractions (OCP); unstable ones are concrete. SDP plus SAP is the DIP for
components: dependencies run toward abstraction. A = Na / Nc (abstract classes and
interfaces over all classes), from 0 to 1
(0,1) stable and abstract
(1,0) unstable, concrete
Zone of Pain
Zone of Uselessness
Zones and metric Zone of Pain (0,0): stable and concrete, rigid (a database schema;
a nonvolatile library such as String is harmless); Zone of Uselessness (1,1):
abstract with no dependents, leftover abstract classes. The Main Sequence joins
(1,0) and (0,1); D = |A + I - 1| (0 on it, 1 farthest); plot D per component, mean
and variance, control limits (D = 0.1 in the Payroll example)
